builder_plan.scenario: Your self-hosted model spends too long generating answers token by token.
builder_plan.change: Check whether a compatible draft model and serving integration exist before renting compute.
builder_plan.baseline: The same target with speculation off, then your existing drafter if you have one.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Accepted draft length, tokens per second, tail latency, output quality, and total GPU cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Speculative Decoding for Mixture-of-Experts Models: Expert Bytes, Kernel Bandwidth and the Best Draft Length
summary: The method modifies the inference engine's speculative verification pass so that each MoE expert selected by multiple drafted tokens is read from memory once instead of once per token, replacing the standard per-slot expert read in engines such as llama.cpp and MLX-LM. It costs engine-level modifications (the authors patched llama.cpp CUDA and Metal and MLX-LM themselves), a per-model bandwidth calibration of under an hour on one expert operation, and added scheduling complexity in the decoding pass. It can fail because the per-slot kernel often has higher effective bandwidth (r = 0.32 to 0.75), making deduplication slower except in a narrow 5-8 token window or never, and the model's own error bounds were violated at 12 of 48 measured points on Metal.
rationale: Adopting this requires self-hosting an MoE model and patching the inference engine's speculative decoding path, and the reported benefit is conditional and narrow, so a small team on one 24 GB GPU or third-party APIs should track it rather than implement it.
technique: Expert-deduplicating speculative decoding for MoE models

claims.statement: The method modifies the inference engine's speculative verification pass so that each MoE expert selected by multiple drafted tokens is read from memory once instead of once per token, replacing the standard per-slot expert read in engines such as llama.cpp and MLX-LM. It costs engine-level modifications (the authors patched llama.cpp CUDA and Metal and MLX-LM themselves), a per-model bandwidth calibration of under an hour on one expert operation, and added scheduling complexity in the decoding pass. It can fail because the per-slot kernel often has higher effective bandwidth (r = 0.32 to 0.75), making deduplication slower except in a narrow 5-8 token window or never, and the model's own error bounds were violated at 12 of 48 measured points on Metal.

Deduplicating expert reads during speculative verification is faster than per-slot reads only when its byte share falls below its bandwidth ratio; on llama.cpp Metal, MLX-LM, and modified llama.cpp CUDA this holds only from 5 to 8 tokens per pass, or never. No end-to-end speedup factor is reported.
